title: Stock up on food to prepare for extreme El Niño weather, minister says
description: Households should stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El Niño event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean, a go
body: Households should stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El Niño event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean, a government minister has said.Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle told the Guardian the powerful natural climate phenomenon will lead to "more extreme storms in this country".Her comments came as the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis.The NAO said the government was too reliant on the private sector to deal with food supply disruption. The government is due to unveil a strategy about preparing for national emergencies later this year.Dame Angela said, external: "We're about to experience probably the largest El Niño that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country."It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously."If you've got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you're going to be a lot better off than if you haven't."So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient."Her comments came as an NAO report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather.It also cited climate change as a longer-term chronic risk which could leave Britain's food supply at risk.The disruptions could push up prices and leave vulnerable people struggling to buy food, it said.The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) was too reliant on private companies to handle disruptions to food supply. It added the department had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland, Sweden and European Union nations, the NAO added.It said ministers should encourage households to prepare for supply chain disruptions and learn from the approaches taken by other countries.Defra said the report showed food supply risks were becoming more complex and the government was working with farmers and industry to strengthen the UK's resilience."While our food businesses and supermarkets have continued to feed the nation through significant disruption, we will carefully consider the report's findings and recommendations as part of our ongoing work to build a more resilient, productive and sustainable food system," a spokesperson said.In July, the government announced plans to set out the "small but important steps" households can take to prepare for food and water shortages in the event of extreme weather or cyber-attacks. These will form a strategy to be unveiled by the end of 2026 aimed at bringing the UK closer into line with European countries in terms of emergency preparedness. Phil Pluck, chief executive of the Cold Chain Federation, the body which represents firms transporting temperature-controlled foods, said Britain was "pretty close to crisis".He told the BBC's Wake Up to Money programme that the country was being targeted by Russian cyber-hackers who "know that there are pinch points in the food supply system".He added that El Niño, as well as global shipping disruption and the threat of pandemics, mean you cannot "just rely on the private sector coming through every single time".Asked whether people should be stocking up in case of disruptions, Pluck added: "Yes, we should."There should be some sensible stocking in each household. And the government in the autumn will be telling all of us to do that."

schema.headline: Stock up on food to prepare for extreme El Niño weather, minister says

title: Nigel Farage unveils small boats deal with Jordan Bardella at Reform conference
description: Farage unveils small boats deal with French National Rally partyImage source, EPA/ShutterstockByBecky MortonPolitical reporterUpdated Just nowNigel Fa
body: Farage unveils small boats deal with French National Rally partyImage source, EPA/ShutterstockByBecky MortonPolitical reporterUpdated Just nowNigel Farage has agreed a deal with France's hard-right National Rally (RN) party on returning small boat Channel migrants, should both parties win power.It comes after Reform UK last month announced a plan to intercept boats and return migrants to French ports using the Royal Navy.The proposed agreement with RN states that France would "ordinarily accept" those on board, and then repatriate them to their home country.It was signed at Reform's annual conference in Birmingham by RN President Jordan Bardella, whose party is currently leading in opinion polls ahead of presidential elections in April next year.In a speech in the main conference hall, ahead of the deal being unveiled, Bardella told delegates that an RN government would "do everything in its power to ensure that France is no longer the gateway for illegal migration into the United Kingdom". Hailing Farage as the UK's next prime minister, Bardella pledged to work with a potential future Reform government to tackle illegal migration.The "memorandum of understanding" unveiled at the conference is a political document, but could be developed into a legal agreement between two future governments, if both parties win power.It states: "The United Kingdom will intercept boats which have launched from French shores and entered British territorial waters and will return the persons on board to France. "France will ordinarily accept these persons, who will be repatriated to their home country in accordance with the law in force in France concerning expulsion."Challenged during a news conference over whether the wording "ordinarily" meant some migrants would not be accepted by France, Farage said it was "legalese".He argued the proposals would mean there was "no incentive" to pay a trafficker to cross the Channel, and "in very, very short order the business model is broken".Farage said the "historic document" would "stop the boats forever".Achieving this goal within the first 100 days of a Reform government is one of the party's key pledges.'New Entente Cordiale'Joining Bardella on the stage after his speech, Farage said the deal marked a "new Entente Cordiale" between France and the UK, in reference to a series of agreements in 1904 that paved the way for greater diplomatic cooperation.Unveiling the memorandum, the pair signed a large mock-up of the document to cheers from the audience of Reform members, with one shouting "Vive la France!".Farage has been forging closer ties with Bardella and his party since meeting the politician in London last December.Previously tipped as a potential candidate for the 2027 presidential election, Le Pen has said she wants to make Bardella prime minister if RN wins power.It comes after party leader Le Pen announced in July she would run for the presidency following a Paris appeal court ruling which upheld her conviction for misusing EU funds but shortened her sentence, clearing the path for her to stand.

schema.headline: Nigel Farage unveils small boats deal with Jordan Bardella at Reform conference

title: Richard O'Sullivan: Man About the House star dies aged 82
description: Actor Richard O'Sullivan, whose roles included Robin Tripp in 1970s TV sitcoms Man About the House and Robin's Nest, has died aged 82.He was also know
body: Actor Richard O'Sullivan, whose roles included Robin Tripp in 1970s TV sitcoms Man About the House and Robin's Nest, has died aged 82.He was also known for starring in Doctor at Large, Dick Turpin, and the 1980s sitcom Me and My Girl, alongside Tim Brooke-Taylor, Joanne Ridley and Joan Sanderson.O'Sullivan died surrounded by close family at Brinsworth House, the Royal Variety Charity's care home, in west London where he had lived for 23 years.In a statement, Giles Cooper of the Royal Variety Charity said: "Richard O'Sullivan was a master of effortless charm and impeccable comic timing, bringing pure warmth, wit, and unforgettable joy to millions of living rooms as a true giant of British television."Cooper added Sullivan would be "sorely missed by us all at the Royal Variety Charity". The actor's son James O'Sullivan said in his own statement: "My dad was as funny and charming in real life as he appeared on our TV screens over the years. "Although much of his career happened before I was born, I was fortunate enough to be able to enjoy and witness his incredible talents on the countless re-runs of his shows that made him the respected and loved actor that he was."He thanked the staff at Brinsworth House for their "love, kindness and care". Man About the House co-starred Paula Wilcox, Sally Thomsett, Yootha Joyce and Brian Murphy in six series on ITV. It was about a man sharing a London flat with two single women - quite a daring storyline for that era. In Me and My Girl, he played a widow living with his adolescent daughter. Born in London in 1944, O'Sullivan started his career as a child actor in the 50s and 60s, playing uncredited roles in dramas in 1953.He went on to appear, external in the Children's Film Foundation's first serial production Raiders of the River, and in 1956 he was in Sir Peter Hall's production of Love's Labour's Lost at the Royal Shakespeare Theatre Stratford.He also appeared in 1961 film Spare the Rod, a social commentary drama about a teacher working in a tough, deprived area, starring Max Bygraves and Donald Pleasance. O'Sullivan played a difficult and defiant student in his final year.After gaining steady work in dramatic roles, including 1963's Cleopatra, as Pharoah Ptolemy XIII, which starred Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton, he moved towards comedy, in shows such as The Ronnie Barker Playhouse, in 1968, and The Galton and Simpson Comedy the following year. Ray Galton and Alan Simpson went on to create the sitcoms Hancock's Half Hour and Steptoe and Son.  O'Sullivan was also in two films with Sir Cliff Richard in the 1960s – The Young Ones in 1961 and Wonderful Life in 1964. By 1973, he took his starring role in Man About the House, which was a big success, not least because of its daring plot about a man living with two single women. "The issue was not the living arrangement itself, but what it implied,"  British Comedy Classics said, external of the series."A man sharing a flat with two unmarried women would be read as sexual, and that risked the show being rejected or framed as inappropriate for prime-time viewing."In order to bypass any potential disapproval from their landlords, George and Mildred Roper, who also got their own spin-off TV series, the two women claim their flatmate Robin is gay. Robin keeps up the pretence for their landlords, which created the comedy and made it acceptable watching for a pre-watershed 70s audience. Between 1979 and 1982 he took on the more dramatic titlular role of 18th Century highwayman Dick Turpin, in ITV's series. But by the 80s he returned to sitcoms with Me and My Girl, which ran from 1984 to 1988, and Trouble in Mind in 1991, about a married psychiatrist who is having something of a mid-life crisis. After this his career became much quieter, with an appearance in Noel's House Party and a starring role in a 1996 film called Holed, about a golfing match.In his statement, James O'Sullivan concluded: "Always kind-spirited, good humoured, a doting grandfather and a wonderful dad – I will miss him dearly."

schema.headline: Richard O'Sullivan: Man About the House star dies aged 82

title: Xbox to limit cloud gaming to 15 hours a month for Game Pass users
description: Xbox is introducing strict monthly time limits for Game Pass subscribers who stream games online through its cloud gaming service.The changes, which c
body: Xbox is introducing strict monthly time limits for Game Pass subscribers who stream games online through its cloud gaming service.The changes, which come into effect in November, will see a subscriber to the  £16.99 Ultimate monthly plan able to stream games for up to 15 hours a month - before having to purchase additional cloud play time.Xbox said the limits were due to the rising cost of cloud gaming, and they would allow the firm to "continue to invest" in the service's "reliability and performance". While some questioned, external whether the service was used by many to begin with, others called out, external the additional limits for subscribers.Cloud gaming allows players to stream and play games online from a remote server using a phone, tablet or controller, rather than downloading and running it on a PC or console at home.Different tiers of subscription to Game Pass will have different limits.Premium users will get 10 hours, while those on the basic Essential tier will get five hours a month before they have to pay for extra time.Xbox claimed just 4% of the people who use Games Pass - its Netflix-style subscription plan for games - use its cloud gaming service.A recent Wall Street Journal article, external reported Game Pass has 30 million subscribers, which would leave the number of people affected by the cloud gaming changes at roughly 1.2 million."This is a pretty awful change, hopefully Xbox adds an extra zero on the end cause 15hrs is abysmal. 30 minutes a day, really?" posted one commenter on X, external.Jez Corden of Windows Central told the BBC the announcement showed that "absolutely nothing is safe from the AI-driven component crisis," but he added it also highlighted "where Microsoft's priorities are".Both cloud gaming and AI use data centres to process information."For them to continue to offer unlimited access to Microsoft Copilot [AI] for free but restrict paid cloud gaming in this way shows some contradiction," he added.Xbox said in a blog post, external that from November, users would also be able to use the company's cloud gaming feature without subscribing to Game Pass, but by buying "cloud playtime hours" through the Xbox store.It has not revealed how much extra hours of cloud gaming would cost.The news comes as Asha Sharma, Xbox's chief executive, told the BBC in an exclusive recent interview that the company and the industry as a whole needed to "start to innovate on affordability and efficiency," amid a "crisis" in computing prices."As an industry, we're in the middle of 'Rampocalypse'. We're in the middle of people coming back from Covid and the patterns changing," she said."Rampocalypse" refers to the fact that the cost of a previously cheap hardware component, random access memory (Ram), has shot up in price with the expansion of compute-hungry data centres. Some people also call it "Ramageddon".Sharma added: "Within Xbox, we haven't been healthy. And so a lot of the reset that will take us throughout the year is really meant to help ensure that we are here for the next 25 years and we're continuing to serve our purpose and our mission."According to Xbox owner Microsoft's July financial filings, external, annual Xbox revenue dropped by $1.7bn to roughly $21.8bn (£16.1bn) - a 7% decline from 2025.Part of Sharma's reset has seen 3,200 people let go at the company - with 1,600 job losses announced in July, and the remaining posts to go gradually over the course of Microsoft's 2027 financial year.Studios which had been acquired by Xbox - including Compulsion Games, which made the Bafta-winning South of Midnight and Double Fine Productions, makers of Psychonauts - were also made independent again.Sharma is betting these changes can reverse its fortunes despite concerns over its subscription strategy and rising AI-related costs."Sometimes you have to restructure a business when it's not doing well, and that was true with our Xbox business," Microsoft's president Brad Smith recently told the BBC.

schema.headline: Xbox to limit cloud gaming to 15 hours a month for Game Pass users

title: 'It's like layer upon layer of miracles': How Nepal flood survivors were rescued from tunnel
description: 'Layer upon layer of miracles' to find tunnel survivors, Nepal rescue adviser tells BBCFigure caption, Watch: Moment workers are rescued from Nepal tu
body: 'Layer upon layer of miracles' to find tunnel survivors, Nepal rescue adviser tells BBCFigure caption, Watch: Moment workers are rescued from Nepal tunnelByTessa WongAsia Digital ReporterA tunnelling expert involved in the rescue operation at a blocked Nepalese hydropower tunnel has described to the BBC how they managed to reach survivors.Arnold Dix has been advising Nepal's hydropower authorities on how to dig through the blocked tunnel to Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, which was one of several stations hit by last week's massive flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border."It's like layer upon layer of miracles" that they found two men on Friday, he said, given the multiple challenges that they faced.The first hurdle was to locate the entrance to the tunnel, in a landscape rendered nearly unrecognisable by the flood that has so far killed 1,300 people."I've never known a rescue operation where you had to look for an entrance of a tunnel that was previously up the hill, that was now underground. You can imagine the enormity of the avalanche, it completely buried the entrance," said Dix, who is the president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association.Using engineering techniques, old topographic maps, satellite imagery of the area after the disaster, video footage from helicopters and "anything else we could find on the surface of the mountain such as power poles", Dix and his team triangulated the likely position of the entrance and started digging.They found it - but the next challenge was to locate the survivors."We knew they would be up ahead, but we didn't know where exactly. So you just have to start digging in the right direction. And you listen out if you can hear anybody," he said.Rescuers had to get through a tunnel blocked entirely by mud and rocks - some bigger than cars - and had to use explosives to clear the way, something they would "normally never do because of the risk of blowing up people [trapped in the tunnel] and blowing ourselves up," Dix said. He credited the Nepalese army for doing "a wonderful job" in managing the explosions with precision to ensure they would not destabilise the tunnel.At the same time, they discovered it was still full of water. Using excavators and pumping machines, Nepalese rescuers dug a series of trenches from the tunnel all the way to the river outside, so they could drain the water.Image source, Nepalese Prime Minister's OfficeImage caption, Rescuers found a substantial amount of water in the tunnel as they dug through itFinally, they had to dig a passageway, "a tiny tunnel the size of a person", through the debris at the top of the tunnel.The advantage of this location "is that you can use the original tunnel's roof as your little tunnel's roof. Also, it mitigates risk of flooding," Dix explained.In the early hours of Friday morning, rescuers heard what they thought could be voices.According to local reports, they called out "don't worry, we're here to rescue you" - and heard back a faint "okay". Shortly after that, they pulled out Sanjaya Shah and Kabir Maharjan, alive.But with dozens of people still thought to be trapped inside the tunnel, the work is far from over.Rescuers heading to 'Goldilocks zone'Dix estimated that they had dug about 60m from the entrance by now, and they would need to dig another 150m more to reach the hydropower station located deep inside the mountain.Rescuers are hoping that the debris from the flood did not reach the station, because if it did, "there would be all kinds of complications - anybody in the station could have been hit by rocks and mud or it could be flooded".The team on the ground are still facing significant dangers."Up ahead, even now, we might run into water which would drown the people tunnelling," Dix said. "And we also have the risk of another flood outside happening, so water could come from behind. So there's the risk of facing water on both ends."But, buoyed by Friday's successful rescue, the team is now hopeful it will reach more survivors in time. "It's a big relief, that we are on the right track. And it gives us renewed energy that our thinking [on how to conduct the rescue] works... we have never done something like this before."Dix said they are now heading towards what he called the "Goldilocks zone" which would be "more friendly to life".This zone is at the uppermost level of the hydropower station where there is some space where survivors may be located. "We got two people out. If we were playing at a casino, some might say it's time to walk away, but we say game on, time to take on the house."Image source, Nepalese Prime Minister's OfficeImage caption, Rescuers had to pull the survivors through a tiny passageway created at the top of the rubble in the tunnel

schema.headline: 'It's like layer upon layer of miracles': How Nepal flood survivors were rescued from tunnel

title: Man who died near Notting Hill Carnival is named
description: The IOPC is appealing for information or any video footage from members of the public or from nearby properties, boats and barges.The police watchdog
body: The IOPC is appealing for information or any video footage from members of the public or from nearby properties, boats and barges.The police watchdog has urged the public not to speculate about Kelly's death.Amanda Rowe, IOPC director of engagement, said: "Our thoughts are with the family and loved ones of Karnell Kelly and everyone affected by his death."We need to independently establish the exact circumstances of this incident given that he has died following an interaction with police officers."Officers made more than 600 arrests during Notting Hill Carnival over the weekend, the Met said.Hundreds of thousands of revellers attended the event in west London over the weekend, and people in costumes and steel bands moved through the streets as the carnival celebrated its 60th anniversary.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

title: England cricket squads: Aneurin Donald and Henry Crocombe called up for Sri Lanka series
description: England have named the uncapped Aneurin Donald and Henry Crocombe in their squads for the white-ball series against Sri Lanka.Opener Donald has been i
body: England have named the uncapped Aneurin Donald and Henry Crocombe in their squads for the white-ball series against Sri Lanka.Opener Donald has been included in the 16-player squad for the T20 series, while seamer Crocombe makes the 16-man line-up for the one-day internationals.England men's national selector Marcus North said the pair are "two promising players who have earned their places on the back of impressive performances in domestic cricket". He added: "Aneurin has had an exceptional season for Derbyshire in the Vitality Blast and also with Trent Rockets in The Hundred while Henry is a player we have had an eye on all summer."England all-rounder Jacob Bethell "underwent successful surgery on his injured knee earlier this week" and is targeting the white-ball series against Australia in November for his comeback.Durham seamer Brydon Carse has not been included in either squad. The 31-year-old was dropped for the second Test of the current series against Pakistan after he was briefly arrested following an incident outside a Derby nightclub on 22 August.

schema.headline: England cricket squads: Aneurin Donald and Henry Crocombe called up for Sri Lanka series

title: Falkland Islands: UK support 'unwavering' after Argentina restates claims
description: More than 40 years after the war over the territory, sovereignty of the archipelago in the south-west Atlantic Ocean remains hotly disputed between Br
body: More than 40 years after the war over the territory, sovereignty of the archipelago in the south-west Atlantic Ocean remains hotly disputed between Britain and Argentina.However in a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.When asked about if the prime minister believed the UK had the necessary forces to defend the sovereignty of the islands the spokesperson said "they will remain so far as long as the islanders wish"."Our armed forces are on standby 24/7 to protect the UK and our interests", the spokesperson added.Announcing his plan for sanctions in a national address on Thursday, Milei reiterated that the Falkland Islands were "historically and legally" Argentinian.He said: "There can be no argument. They are part of the Argentine territory."The islanders on their usurped territory do not have a legitimate right to self-determination and any argument on any such self-determination is invalid."Milei described the Sea Lion oilfield as a "clear and present danger", and said if Argentina does not act swiftly, "they will have the material capacity to access the oil that lies underneath our sea – something that has never happened before."He continued: "The Falklands are our future, we need to recover these islands which are nationally relevant. There is no other path forward".It is not yet clear how or to what extent the sanctions will be imposed or tightened. In Argentina, a current law already allows for restrictions of activities of oil companies participating in projects considered unauthorised on the islands.Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting oil in the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, something Milei said Argentina could not allow.A joint statement from the two firms on Friday said it had the valid licences granted by the government of the Falkland Islands, "and with the full support of the UK government." The project is due to deliver its first oil in 2028, Rockhopper and Navitas said the partnerships' timetable would not be affected.  The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles from the islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil - described by Rockhopper as a field containing "highly marketable crude".Milei also announced plans for a naval base in Tierra del Fuego in the south of Argentina, saying Trump and the US were "assessing their historical position in regard to the Falklands", which Argentina refers to as Las Malvinas."That is not empty words as they understand that Argentina is a reliable partner and a valuable ally for decades to come," he said, describing the UK as a nation "in decline".On Thursday, President Trump hinted the US would not help the UK in any future Falklands conflict because Britain "had not been there to help me" during his war with Iran.Trump's latest remarks on the islands come after he previously said the US position on the Falklands is one of many under review.On Friday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK would "resolutely uphold" the self-determination of the islands.Writing on X on Friday, Miliband said the Islands would remain British as that is the "overwhelming position of the islanders." Defence Secretary Wes Streeting also said Britain's commitment to the Falkland Islands was "absolute and unshakeable"."Milei's statement overnight tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands," he wrote in his own post on X.In an earlier statement, Downing Street said it was "not the first time" the Argentine government had made economic threats against the Falkland Islands. "We are clear that the Falkland Islanders' right of self-determination extends to the right to exploit their own natural resources," it said. Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said "Britain does not surrender to bullies". "If (Milei) wants a stronger Argentina, he should build its economy, not threaten others." Although the US is formally neutral, Washington provided support for Britain's campaign to retake the islands after the Argentinian invasion in 1982.Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them.The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.In a sign of the ongoing tensions between the two countries over the issue, Argentina players celebrated their victory over England in the World Cup by waving a banner in support of their country's territorial claim.

schema.headline: Falkland Islands: UK support 'unwavering' after Argentina restates claims

title: Five jailed after Lincolnshire kidnap victim jumped from window
description: Five people have been jailed after a man jumped from a first-floor window to escape kidnappers.The victim was lured to a property in Market Rasen in J
body: Five people have been jailed after a man jumped from a first-floor window to escape kidnappers.The victim was lured to a property in Market Rasen in July 2025 because of  "personal matters linked to a past relationship breakdown", Lincolnshire Police said.The force said he was "repeatedly assaulted, threatened, humiliated and tormented by his captors, while those involved filmed the abuse on their mobile phones and laughed as it unfolded".After being held overnight he was driven to a house in Lincoln, where he was caught on CCTV leaping into a tree and climbing down before running into the street and flagging down a passing police car.Armed police intercepted two of the kidnappers in a car, and the others were arrested at the house in Market Rasen.The gang were jailed at Lincoln Crown Court on 28 August.Brad'Lee Ranyard, 20, of Portland Street, Lincoln, was jailed for nine years after being convicted of kidnap and pleading guilty to false imprisonment.Jackson Nicholson, 25, of Lindsey Drive, Gainsborough, was also jailed for nine years after being convicted of kidnap and pleading guilty to false imprisonment and possessing a bladed object in public.Craig Ranyard, 42, of Barsey Walk, Horncastle, was sentenced to five years and three months in prison after pleading guilty to false imprisonment Danielle Thompson, 38, of Lime Walk, Market Rasen, was given four years and nine months after pleading guilty to false imprisonment.Nathan Gladwell, 36, of Union Street, Market Rasen, was sent to prison for three years and seven months after pleading guilty to false imprisonment.Det Con Liam Henderson said: "This was a sustained and deeply distressing ordeal in which a man was subjected to violence, threats and humiliation at the hands of people who appeared to find amusement in his suffering."The victim showed remarkable courage in seizing the opportunity to escape. The CCTV footage captures a desperate moment in which he quite literally risked everything to get away from those holding him captive."Listen to highlights from Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds, and watch the latest episode of Look North.

schema.headline: Five jailed after Lincolnshire kidnap victim jumped from window

title: Jackdaw gas field set to be approved as soon as mid-September, sources say
description: Controversial Jackdaw gas field set to be approved in weeks, sources sayImage caption, The Jackdaw gas platform and drilling rig stand east of Aberdee
body: Controversial Jackdaw gas field set to be approved in weeks, sources sayImage caption, The Jackdaw gas platform and drilling rig stand east of Aberdeen in the North SeaBySimon JackBusiness editorUpdated 9 hours agoThe UK government is set to give the go-ahead for a controversial new gas field off the coast of Aberdeen, the BBC understands.Approval for the Jackdaw project could come in mid-September, just before  Parliament breaks for party conference season, according to government and industry sources.The gas field was approved by the former Conservative government in 2022 but was delayed by a legal ruling from a Scottish court, after environmental groups argued consent was given without fully considering the climate impact.Jackdaw's owner says it will account for 6% of UK gas output when at peak production but environmental groups say it will provide only 2% of UK use when imports are included.Campaigners launched legal challenges after Jackdaw was approved in 2022 and when the Rosebank oil field off Shetland was given the green light in 2023.The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites.A judge ruled that more detailed climate assessments had to be published, and further estimates were put out for consultation in July.Both Jackdaw and Rosebank are operated by Adura, a joint venture between energy giants Shell and Norway's Equinor. Aberdeen-based firm Ithaca also owns 20% of Rosebank.Adura has estimated that Jackdaw could produce 35.8m tonnes of carbon over its 11-year lifetime, the equivalent of 90% of Scotland's emissions for 2023. But it said a more likely estimate was about 23.6m tonnes - equivalent to 60% of the 2023 figure.Environmentalists insist that more drilling would be unconscionable, hampering efforts to cut planet-warming carbon emissions as deadly heatwaves and extreme weather affect billions across the globe.They also say starting production would not protect energy security and that transitioning sooner to greener technologies would be better for supporting jobs.But industry bodies argue that starting production at the sites would provide much-needed jobs and improve the UK's energy security as overseas conflicts threaten supply.Advocates of the project also told the BBC that Jackdaw's output is critical to extending the life of other North Sea infrastructure including Shearwater - a large offshore oil and gas production hub that processes hydrocarbons before piping them to coastal refineries and terminals.Adura said that if approval comes in September, the field could start delivering gas to UK homes by this winter as the construction is "99% complete".A public consultation on the future of Jackdaw and another new oil field, Rosebank, closed in August and the decision now rests with Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.Speaking in the House of Commons on Thursday, Energy Minister Kate White said that the energy secretary would make separate decisions on the two sites, but gave no indication of the timings of an announcement."The process ended in August, and the Secretary of State will be taking those decisions in due course," she told MPs.Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently said there needs to be a "pragmatic approach" towards domestic oil and gas. "We won't be able to stop using oil and gas for some time. That's just a fact," he said."The question is whether we can accelerate use of it so that we pay for the transition."Unlike North Sea oil, most of which is exported and then reimported in various refined forms, almost all North Sea gas is used domestically in the UK.The UK is heavily reliant on gas imports with over 60% imported from Norway and the United States.Wholesale natural gas prices have surged this year as a result of the Iran war and are currently at a three-year high, prompting concerns over energy security.Gas storage levels in Europe are significantly lower than usual for this time of year after countries delayed stockpiling in the summer in the hope that the conflict would end before winter and prices would in turn fall.They face the prospect of rushing to buy gas now or paying potentially higher prices when the winter comes.Prices are set internationally and a green light to Jackdaw would not lower the cost of gas for domestic consumers. But extracting gas domestically creates lower greenhouse gas emissions than liquefying, shipping and regasifying liquid natural gas (LNG) imported from other countries.Chris O'Shea, the boss of British Gas owner Centrica, said any additional domestic gas supply would reduce Britain's reliance on imported fossil fuels, "so it's got to be good".He told the BBC's Today programme: "It wouldn't lower the cost materially, but basic economics would tell you that if you've got a fixed demand for a product and you increase the supply, the price should move."He also pointed to the high tax rates on profits from North Sea oil and gas, adding that the new extraction would give the government more money to spend.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Campaigners in London in July urged Andy Burnham not to open the North Sea to new projectsTessa Khan, executive director of environmental group Uplift which brought the legal challenge, said more North Sea drilling would not cut energy bills and would "make no meaningful difference" to UK energy supply."The science is clear that the world already has far more oil and gas than can ever be safely burned if we are to limit warming," she added."When it comes to these decisions, the prime minister needs to listen to scientists warnings and think back to those families who lost their homes to this summer's wildfires, the UK farmers struggling to grow our food in the drought, and the lives lost in the floods in Nepal – and not the self-interested demands of the oil companies."The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said it does not comment on speculation.A spokesman added: "The North Sea remains a vital national asset and oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come - alongside transitioning to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis."Any decision will take into account all relevant evidence, including environmental assessments and public representations received during the consultation process."Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: Jackdaw gas field set to be approved as soon as mid-September, sources say

title: Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage and Russia is the chief suspect
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Germany said the attack at Leipzig airport was part of a pattern of "Russian hybrid operations" in EuropeBySarah R
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Germany said the attack at Leipzig airport was part of a pattern of "Russian hybrid operations" in EuropeBySarah RainsfordSouthern and Eastern Europe correspondentUpdated 1 hour agoAs summer temperatures in Europe smashed records and many politicians shifted to holiday mode, Russia remained focused on its war.Not only did its military attacks across Ukraine intensify last month, becoming ever more deadly for civilians, Russia also appears to have escalated its sabotage campaign across Europe.This time, military and defence sector sites were the prime target.A full month after drones packed with explosives were found at Leipzig's airport, used by Ukraine to transport military goods, Germany's interior minister has declared that "Russia is responsible".Russia's President Vladimir Putin is demanding proof, as always, and his officials call the accusation "absurd".But the drones were just a dramatic start. August then brought a series of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia.Some of the affected countries have already blamed Russia; others are still investigating and some fires may eventually be ruled accidental, exactly as such attacks are designed to seem.Poland's interior minister is clear."There are many, many signals that Russia is changing its strategy and intensifying its activities, including terrorist and sabotage activities," Marcin Kierwiński said, warning people to be on their guard.August campaign across Europe4 August Germany: The first drone at Leipzig airport is discovered.10 August Bulgaria: A major fire breaks out at a warehouse of defence firm EMCO in Tryavna. In a statement, the company recalled previous blasts at its facilities which were investigated for links to Russia. "Human error is excluded," it said.13 August Italy: A fire at KNDS Ammo Italy outside Rome triggers a large explosion. The local prosecutor is looking into possible outside interference, La Repubblica newspaper reports. Publicly, his office will only confirm that a case has been opened for negligent disaster against "unknown persons".15 August Estonia: The Milrem Robotics factory in Tallinn, which the Kyiv Post says supplies drones to Ukraine, goes up in flames. Two suspects are arrested.Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal says the possibility of Russian sabotage is being "taking seriously" by investigators.25 August Slovakia: Police announce they have averted an arson attack on a Ukrainian-owned drone manufacturer and seized a "large amount of incendiary mixture". The firm itself blames Russia and police arrest three suspects who they say were "following orders". Slovakia is Russia's close ally in Europe.30 August Poland: A country which is heavily targeted for sabotage reports two more fires. One is in Lublin at a company which produces helicopter components. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said arson "cannot be ruled out". An attack on the drone producer, WB Group, is clearer cut. A masked man is caught on CCTV throwing incendiary devices. Tusk calls it a "continuation of Russia's escalatory activities".The pattern has continued into September with two Bulgarians arrested in Munich, Germany, for suspected arson after throwing incendiary devices from a car at defence firm Rhode & Schwartz.Image source, EPAImage caption, The 31 August fire at Skarżysko-Kamienna targeted one of Poland's biggest defence firmsWhy is this happening now?Attacks on military and defence targets are not new, although previous acts of sabotage linked to Russia include more puzzling targets - such as an Ikea store and a Polish paint store.The novelty now is the concentration of cases."The intensity of military sites being attacked we've seen over the past couple of weeks is unusual," Daniela Richterova of the Department of War Studies at King's College says.She links the spike to developments in Russia's invasion of Ukraine."We've basically seen Ukraine take the war to Russia and strike deep inside Russian territory…They [Moscow] are under pressure, they have to do something."Whilst some sabotage is staged to sow chaos or fear, Richterova believes the Kremlin's aim right now is "coercive signalling": pressuring countries to stop supporting Kyiv by raising the stakes. After a slow start, Germany is Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid.There are other theories.To some, Russia is less concerned about "turning off the taps" of supplies to Ukraine and more about testing Nato for weaknesses."Russia is probing the boundaries of what's acceptable and collecting information on the results. They find out what works, and what's vulnerable," argues Keir Giles from the Chatham House think tank.He sees the sabotage campaign as preparation for the "next phase", as he puts it, of Russia's aggression in Europe."They're assessing the willingness of the victim country to actually do something about it."The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), which tracks sabotage cases, points to a previous surge in 2024 when Ukraine's allies began allowing it to use Western-supplied weapons deeper inside Russia.2024 was the year of the parcel bomb plot, when Russia was accused of sending packages containing liquid explosive to the UK and Poland. One ignited shortly before it was loaded on to a DHL cargo plane. It is thought this was a test run for something significantly bigger.Image source, Police handoutImage caption, Four parcels were sent from Lithuania to the UK and Poland in 2024 - two caught fire, at a warehouse in the UK and at Leipzig's airport"That was a marked high in terms of their willingness to inflict mass casualties," Giles adds.It was a step so serious, the White House contacted the Kremlin to tell it to stop. Russia had probed and found the limit.But the attacks have continued. German media on Friday quoted a federal police report that lists more than 165 suspected sabotage cases nationwide this year, though they don't say who is responsible.Who are the suspected saboteurs?Reports from Germany suggest the men who loaded and launched the drones at Leipzig's airport were Russian, and at least one may have entered the country specially for this job.That would be unusual.The vast majority of sabotage attacks in Europe have been carried out by Russian proxies: its so-called "gig economy saboteurs".They are usually Russian-speakers from former Soviet states, recruited online and driven by the cash, not political conviction.In one case the BBC reported from Poland, the saboteurs-for-hire had previously fought for Ukraine as volunteers.The "handlers" are generally thought to remain in Russia, co-ordinating operations online.The IISS likened the proxies they used to kamikaze drones: cheap and easy to launch in large numbers, but disposable.The amateurs can be sloppy or reckless, though. In the parcel plot, one man failed to find a pick-up point and the whole mission had to be aborted.So if Moscow did send professionals for the Leipzig drone launch, it suggests it wanted precision - and success.In fact, the devices appear to have malfunctioned.Nato faced with Soviet-style campaignRussia's sabotage operations seem to come from the Cold War playbook. Daniela Richterova's research shows very similar targets on Soviet sabotage lists, and agents-saboteurs were used in much the same way.The idea, she says, was to have small, deniable attacks in peace-time that would escalate in times of war."I think we are still in the grey zone between the two, but the kind of attacks we've seen in the past weeks shrink that zone," she says. "And I think that increases the risk of what happens next."As Nato scrambles to respond, questions like how many small, individual attacks add up to a sustained Russian assault - and demand action - remain unanswered.Perhaps riskier than all is the potential for escalation by accident.What if the exploding parcel had gone off mid-air and caused a crash? What if the Leipzig drone had brought down a plane?"I think it could result in a big attack," Richterova says. "Then Nato, in this heightened security environment, would not be able to ignore that, and have to react."

schema.headline: Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage and Russia is the chief suspect

title: Italian Grand Prix: Charles Leclerc leads Lewis Hamilton in first practice
description: Lando Norris was sixth quickest for McLaren but the world champion, who has won the past two races in Hungary and Zandvoort, ended up following Antone
body: Lando Norris was sixth quickest for McLaren but the world champion, who has won the past two races in Hungary and Zandvoort, ended up following Antonelli and the Williams of Carlos Sainz across the gravel at the Turn One chicane. Russell and Leclerc also tested the limits of the famous circuit, while other drivers highlighted issues with traffic over the team radio. Briton Arvid Lindblad was behind Norris in seventh place for Racing Bulls, with Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto, Alpine's Franco Colapinto and rookie Paul Aron, replacing Colapinto's team-mate Pierre Gasly for the first hour, completing the top 10. The other McLaren of Oscar Piastri ended the session 11th and more than four tenths off his team-mate Norris. Japanese driver Yuki Tsunoda is replacing Lawson for a second race weekend in a row at Racing Bulls and finished 12th, above Audi's Nico Hulkenberg in 13th and the Haas of Oliver Bearman in 14th. During the session, it was announced McLaren and Red Bull have won their appeals against the result of the Monaco Grand Prix after a controversy over multiple incorrect pit-lane speeding penalties.The victory means Alpine's Pierre Gasly loses the podium he was awarded after an appeal by the French team that overturned two five-second penalties.

title: Rangers-Celtic: No away fans for SPFL Old Firm matches this season
description: There will be no away supporters for Celtic and Rangers derbies in the Scottish Premiership or Premier Sports Cup this season.The "temporary arrangeme
body: There will be no away supporters for Celtic and Rangers derbies in the Scottish Premiership or Premier Sports Cup this season.The "temporary arrangement" was reached following talks between the Glasgow clubs and the Scottish Professional Football League (SPFL).It follows the Scottish FA's independent review into events surrounding last term's Scottish Cup quarter-final at Ibrox, which was marred by unrest and pitch incursions from both sets of fans.Rangers host Celtic in the Premier Sports Cup on 13 September, with the city rivals meeting at Celtic Park in the league a week later.Rangers had proposed a reduced away allocation of 300 for the impending cup tie,  with Celtic rejecting the offer.The crowd disorder on 8 March came after a penalty shootout win for Celtic, when around 8,000 visiting supporters had been present. That figure was much larger than recent Old Firm league derbies, with ticketing rules different for the Scottish Cup.The Scottish FA announced last month that both clubs would have to play their next Scottish Cup home games behind closed doors.Announcing the measures, a statement from the SPFL said: "This temporary arrangement will allow both clubs, together with the SPFL, Police Scotland and other relevant stakeholders, to give proper consideration to the findings and recommendations of the independent review, take forward the necessary actions and ensure sufficient time is available to plan future fixtures thoroughly."It will also provide greater certainty for supporters and those involved in matchday planning, while avoiding repeated uncertainty around ticketing arrangements for individual fixtures."All parties have committed to working constructively during this period, with safety and security remaining the priority."The March cup meeting was the first time Celtic supporters have been given the full Broomloan Road Stand allocation at Ibrox since away allocations were reduced to fewer than 1,000 in 2018.The number of away fans at both Ibrox and Celtic Park fluctuated between about 800 and zero in a series of tit-for-tat moves before an arrangement was reached for "around 5%" capacity [2,500 - 3,000] for league games in 2025 and 2026.Rangers manager Derek McInnes described the news as "disappointing", saying: "It's always better when opposition fans are allowed into a derby game."In the context of everything that's gone on with this fixture and the last part of it, I think there's a lot to consider and a lot to discuss."As far as I was led to believe, that was still up for discussion, so it's kind of caught me on the hop a wee bit."Celtic manager Martin O'Neill described the decision as "inevitable" and "really sad".O'Neill added: "It's a great, great fixture when the ground is absolutely full. And I think the away fans make this."Hopefully the two clubs will maybe get together at some stage or another and try to iron out the particular problems."

title: US Open 2026: Naomi Osaka and Jessica Pegula on influencers causing disruption in New York
description: Lights. Camera. Quiet please...When it comes to etiquette in tennis, there are a fair few unwritten rules.Apologising after winning a point from a net
body: Lights. Camera. Quiet please...When it comes to etiquette in tennis, there are a fair few unwritten rules.Apologising after winning a point from a net cord. Honesty around line calls, double bounces and double-hits. Post-match handshakes. As for the spectators, it is common courtesy not to disturb the players during points.Around 100 influencers and content creators have been granted accreditation for the tournament in New York - double the amount from last year.Their presence has led to debate over how to balance bringing tennis to a new, different audience while respecting the game's etiquette."I definitely think it's cool to have a new demographic and I definitely think it helps grow the sport," world number four Coco Gauff said."But if you're being invited to a red carpet, you wouldn't show up in jeans."I think it's just follow the etiquette of the sport. That's all."During two-time champion Naomi Osaka's first-round match on Arthur Ashe Stadium, one group held a photo shoot in their hospitality suite while play was going on.The group turned on a portable ring light while Osaka was serving, leading to a reprimand from the umpire.When Osaka returned on Thursday, the umpire had to remind the crowd several times to be quiet."Today the umpire told everyone to be quiet more than I've ever heard an umpire tell a crowd to be quiet," Osaka said."I tell people I normally just focus on the match and the court, but there was a moment where there was people shouting and you could hear it quite clearly."I think it bothered my opponent, too."In one video, which has gone viral, a group can be seen speaking loudly as they film themselves during Osaka's first-round match on Tuesday, which led to the chair umpire calling for them to stop."I think obviously if you come to a sporting event, you have to respect the sport," Osaka said."I feel like it's common courtesy to read up on the sport, especially the etiquette."It could be a good thing for people to make the sport of tennis popular to their specific audience, but I think it has to be managed a lot better, especially in the situation like my first-round match."Overall, I think there are huge positives. You want people to continue to grow the sport. "I just think it has to be in a way that everyone knows the rules and the etiquette."Arthur Ashe is the biggest tennis stadium in the world, and matches are often accompanied by a buzz of noise from conversations around the arena.Some players love it. Some do not.Men's seventh seed Daniil Medvedev, who has had a tricky relationship with the New York crowds in the past, believes whatever brings more eyes to tennis can only be a good thing."I think the more we try to raise awareness about tennis, the better it is, the more popular the sport is," the Russian said."The more the sport grows, the better it is. I trust USTA [tournament organisers the United States Tennis Association] with what they are doing. "I think [there is] a lot more upside than downside, so go for it."American 11th seed Frances Tiafoe praised the diversity of the crowd in New York."I think the Open is great because you get all types of people that want to come and watch tennis," he said."All different walks of life, different types of people, different type of occupations. Personally, I love that."I have no problem with anybody doing anything, coming to watch the tennis."American world number three Jessica Pegula, however, said some of the behaviour had been "disrespectful"."I can appreciate the influencers coming and showcasing the US Open experience," Pegula said."But I do think that it's tough when you see videos when they're taking pictures and using the selfie lights."People are down there trying to perform. It's their career and their job. It seems a bit disrespectful."I think it's become a little too much this year. "I can appreciate one side of it, but I think when you have the other side literally interrupting matches, it gets a little tough."The US Open introduced a policy of free fan movement in 2024, meaning fans no longer have to wait to take their seats during changeovers.A year later, the tournament was expanded to 15 days. The week before the singles draw is now marketed as a 'Fan Week', showcasing the revamped mixed doubles competition and exhibition matches between players past and present.It is all part of what tournament chief executive Craig Tiley hopes will become "the tennis Disneyland".Tiley, asked about influencers being accredited in a pre-tournament news conference, said: "We need to find ways of reaching new audiences, reaching people in a way that they connect with media today."The creation of the creator credential has been a key part of that because it's enabled us to talk to people in a way that they're listening. That's been a big focus."Since the incident in Osaka's first match, there has been increased messaging on screens around the ground reminding people to "refrain from any activity that could disrupt the game, including noise levels, flash photography and ring lights".The USTA said in a statement it "is always striving to grow tennis in this country and bring new audiences into the sport"."We want all of our fans and guests to have an incredible time when they attend, but we also need to ensure they do not interfere with the action and competition on the court," it added."We are continually looking for ways to ensure fans in the stands know what is permitted and what is prohibited."

title: Bristol woman whose XL bully killed her cousin given suspended prison sentence
description: Image source, Avon and Somerset PoliceImage caption, Kelcie Reed, 24, admitted being in charge of an XL bully that killed her teenage cousinByChloe Ha
body: Image source, Avon and Somerset PoliceImage caption, Kelcie Reed, 24, admitted being in charge of an XL bully that killed her teenage cousinByChloe HarcombeReporting fromin Bristol Crown Court and Bea SwallowBristolUpdated 4 hours agoA woman has been given a suspended prison sentence after her XL bully dog attacked and killed her cousin.Kelcie Reed, 24, of Bristol, previously admitted being in charge of a dog dangerously out control, causing the death of Morgan Dorsett.The 19-year-old, from Shrewsbury, died from neck injuries caused by the attack, which happened at Reed's flat in south Bristol in February 2025.At Bristol Crown Court, Judge Anna Richardson sentenced Reed to 18 weeks in prison, suspended for 18 months. She will also be required to undergo mental health treatment.Emergency services were called to the dog attack at a flat in Cobhorn Drive, Bishopsworth, but despite their best efforts, Morgan died from bites to her neck and face, a post-mortem examination ruled.The dog, named Prince, which belonged to Reed and her boyfriend, was sedated at the scene and later "humanely destroyed", police said.Image source, Avon and Somerset PoliceImage caption, Morgan Dorsett, 19, died after the attack in Bristol in February 2025Reed, who appeared emotional throughout the proceedings, wept in the dock as the sentence was read out.The judge told her: "Rather than putting everyone through the additional trauma of a trial, you accepted responsibility."You are someone who has over the last 18 months done what they needed to do to try and move forward. You need to continue to do that."The court heard a post-mortem examination revealed cocaine in Morgan's system, which had caused her to "act erratically"."Morgan's behaviour was unusual, and when she sat up she began to scream upon seeing Prince. That led him to barking and ultimately, he attacked her," Richardson said.The judge also noted Reed had attempted to intervene and stop the attack, suffering cuts and bruises herself, but was ultimately "unsuccessful".Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Kelcie Reed was shielded from the press as she arrived at Bristol Crown Court for sentencingIn a victim impact statement, Morgan's mother Marie Smith said the family now "lives under a shadow", with every major milestone "tainted" without her present.She told the court she struggled to sign birthday cards from the family, leaving an empty spot where her daughter's signature should be."Morgan's death has affected our family so deeply it's hard to put into words who she was and what we've lost," she said."It's something I carry with me all the time. It's impossible not to feel like something's missing. We find ourselves saying 'Morgan would've loved this' in happy moments."I don't think I'll ever be able to fully explain how much this has changed every part of our lives."Image caption, Caeila Dorsett described her older sister as a bubbly and positive personMorgan's younger sister, Caeila Dorsett, described her as a "super bubbly" and sociable person; a "built in best friend" from the day she was born."We did everything together - wore matching outfits, went to the same schools, had all the same friends, even shared a room for 16 years," she told BBC Newsbeat."She was definitely the person to take the good out of every situation and make it the centre. She was the first person I'd tell about anything exciting. "That's what I try and do now, just bring some of Morgan's positivity into my everyday life."'Loopholes' in legislationThe 19-year-old said she initially "felt sorry" for Reed having to witness the fatal attack on a family member, but that in the 18 months since the incident, she felt her cousin had "not shown any remorse or compassion".In her victim impact statement, she told the court: "We continue to live with so many unanswered questions which makes it difficult to find any sense of peace."The family say they are working alongside the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs in a bid to remove "loopholes" from current legislation around banned dog breeds. This will look at, for example, whether a dog is living with someone other than the exemption certificate holder, which can be difficult to track and enforce.PanoramaDangerous Dogs: Is the Ban Working?Det Sgt Rich Glanville from Avon and Somerset Police described the investigation as "complex and challenging", adding it was the "first of its kind" for the force."As police officers we're trained to deal with a multitude of situations, but I don't think something like this could ever be trained for," he said."It was a horrendous incident which cost someone their life, and the impact to the officers and ambulance crew that attended would be something they'll never forget."Image caption, Det Sgt Rich Glanville says Morgan's death was the first time an XL bully had killed someone in the Avon and Somerset areaGlanville said he hoped the primary takeaway from Morgan's death would be one of responsibility for dog owners, to ensure legislation is being followed and suitable precautions are considered."The dog is on the [banned breeds] list for a reason, but owners have to be responsible as well," he said."You have to look at the dog's past to try and truly understand what temperament that dog has, what training that dog has had, and whether you are a suitable person to own that type of dog."If you feel that people are not going to be safe, then you should be taking action."If you are concerned that your dog is becoming dangerous, Glanville advises contacting a vet or specially trained dog liaison officers at the force for advice.Additional reporting by Jared Evitts and Alastair McKeeGet in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Bristol

schema.headline: Bristol woman whose XL bully killed her cousin given suspended prison sentence
